newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: Central Africa's former emperor Bokassa dead.
newsitem.headline: Central Africa's former emperor Bokassa dead.

text.p: Jean-Bedel Bokassa, former self-styled emperor of the Central African Republic, has died at the age of 75, closing a colourful and sometimes grim chapter in the diamond-rich yet impoverished nation's history.

One of Bokassa's sons, Jean Charles, announced the news early on Monday. The flamboyant former leader, whose rule was one of cruelty and extravagance punctuated by capricious decisions, died of a heart attack on Sunday night in Bangui.

Years after he was ousted in 1979, Bokassa was convicted of conspiracy to murder and embezzelement and sentenced to death, a sentence later commuted. One of his cooks told the court that he used to fry human flesh for Bokassa's meals but the emperor was not convicted of cannibalism.

State radio carried a government announcement that Bokassa, who had been ill with kidney, suspected cerebral and other problems, would have a national funeral and broadcast extracts from his speeches interspersed with solemn music.
Jean Charles said Bokassa had been a "good father who always catered for the educational and other needs of his family", notably his children -- of whom he had at least 55.
"My father had nationalist ideas but he was often opposed from the outside where he was portrayed as a monster, an eater of men," he told Reuters.

Bokassa seized power in 1966. Modelling himself on his hero Napoleon Bonaparte of France, he crowned himself emperor in 1977. His crown was worth $5 million and the ceremony reputedly cost a quarter of the nation's annual foreign exchange earnings.
Ousted in a French-backed coup in 1979 while in Libya, he lived in exile in Ivory Coast and former colonial power France.

In 1986 Bokassa suddenly returned to the Central African Republic. He was sentenced to death in 1987 for murder and embezzlement after a trial coloured by tales of infanticide, cannibalism and of human flesh kept in fridges.
The military leader at the time, Andre Kolingba, commuted Bokassa's sentence to life in prison and then freed him in 1993 at the height of a transition to multi-party democracy.

Bokassa's "monarchic and dictatorial regime" caused a lot of harm, opposition Patriotic Front for Progress leader Abel Goumba said, but, echoing many Central Africans who seem to have forgiven and in some cases forgotten his excesses, he added:
"Bokassa played a very important role for his country."
Bokassa remained convinced of his popularity with the masses until the end, harbouring hopes of being allowed to stage a comeback via presidential elections scheduled for 1999.
"Whenever I go out, a large gathering collects about me out of adoration, so I seldom go out," he told Reuters in an interview at his home in the capital Bangui in May.
Around that time he wrote to President Ange-Felix Patasse asking for a formal amnesty so that he could run for president.

"His majesty Bokassa the First hopes that his request will be favourably received to enable him to stand as a candidate in the next presidential elections according to the principle of democracy, in line with the wishes of the majority of the Central African people," he said in the letter.
Bokassa, a fervent Roman Catholic, once flirted with the idea of becoming a priest. Instead he became a soldier in France's colonial army.
He was armed forces chief of staff when he toppled his nephew David Dacko, the nation's independence president.
Bokassa had been receiving medical care at home since returning from treatment in Ivory Coast in October.

Bokassa lived quietly in Bangui on a French army pension following his release from jail but during an army pay revolt in May he joined critics of France, which stepped in under a defence pact to keep Patasse in power.
"Why does France intervene in our country at every little problem, why? Perhaps because of the diamonds," he said.
Tales of gifts of diamonds from Bokassa spiced cover of French President Valery Giscard d'Estaing's 1981 reelection campaign. Some say they contributed to his subsequent defeat.
